title: Daylight street moments
conditions: Bright overcast streets with people walking across the frame; light changes between open sky and building shade.
intent: Keep a brief gesture sharp while retaining enough street context.

setup.focusTarget: Place the tracking zone on the approaching person’s upper body; check that it stays there as they move.
setup.whiteBalance: Auto WB
setup.stabilization: On for handheld; still hold steady.
setup.metering: Multi/evaluative as a reference; check important highlights in the test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Choose 1/500 s and f/5.6; Auto ISO responds to shade. If ISO reaches its ceiling, open to f/4 before slowing the shutter. In strong sun lower ISO is normal.

phone.mode: Photo mode; burst for gestures
phone.aperture: Usually fixed by the selected lens; not user-adjustable.
phone.shutter: Automatic; seek 1/250 s or faster in a manual app
phone.focus: Tap or track the person, not the bright shopfront.
phone.focal: Main 1× lens; move for framing.
phone.guidance: Frame first, wait for someone to enter a clean patch of background, then shoot a short burst.
phone.limitation: Night mode and multi-frame HDR can merge moving limbs; ordinary Photo mode is more reliable for fast gestures.
why: Good daylight gives the automatic camera a better chance of freezing a walking gesture.
The main lens keeps the person connected to the street without the detail loss of heavy digital zoom.
Choosing the background first makes a brief gesture readable even on a small screen.
steps: Choose an uncluttered patch of pavement with good light and keep clear of other people.
Select ordinary Photo mode and the main lens; frame before the person enters.
Tap or track the person if supported, then make a short burst as their stride opens.
Enlarge the face and feet and inspect pale clothing for clipped highlights.
If limbs smear, seek brighter light or a pause; with a manual app, try 1/500 s and let its available ISO control compensate.

optional: Manual app with documented shutter control
Spare power for a long walk

problems.cause: The selected exposure was too long for the walk.
problems.fix: Use brighter light or a pause; if selectable, try 1/500 s and retest.

problems.cause: Focus selected the background.
problems.fix: Tap the person earlier or use person tracking; check the next face enlarged.

problems.cause: The phone brightened important highlights too much.
problems.fix: Reduce the exposure slider slightly and check both face brightness and clothing.

problems.cause: Multi-frame processing combined changing positions.
problems.fix: Try ordinary Photo mode or a short burst; disable optional Night processing and compare results.

phone.tip: Leave a clean gap around the next step, not just around the person’s head.

why: The 1/500 s shutter is the priority because a walker can blur even when buildings are sharp.
f/5.6 gives more tolerance than a wide-open lens when the subject changes distance.
A 35 mm-equivalent view keeps the person connected to the street without forcing a very close viewpoint.
steps: Find a useful background and a clear space for the subject to enter.
Watch the direction of light and keep bright signs away from the face.
Set continuous focus, the chosen shutter and aperture, and an Auto ISO ceiling you accept.
Track a person before the strongest gesture and shoot a brief burst.
Enlarge the face and feet; inspect highlight clipping on pale clothing.
If limbs smear, try 1/1000 s; if focus stayed on the background, reduce the focus area.

problems.cause: Subject motion at the chosen shutter.
problems.fix: Use 1/1000 s and allow a higher ISO.

problems.symptom: Both person and street have a double edge
problems.cause: Camera moved during release.
problems.fix: Brace your elbows and squeeze gently; use a shorter exposure.

problems.cause: AF selected a high-contrast sign.
problems.fix: Use a smaller AF zone and place it on the person before release.

problems.cause: Highlights exceeded the recording range.
problems.fix: With Auto ISO, dial about −0.7 EV if supported; otherwise lower ISO manually and retest.

alternatives.name: Graphic silhouettes
alternatives.effect: People become dark shapes against a sunlit wall.
alternatives.requirements: Direct sun on the background; expose for the wall.

alternatives.name: Busy layered street
alternatives.effect: More near and far activity stays readable.
alternatives.requirements: Use slower walkers or their pauses; allow Auto ISO to rise in shade.

tip: Choose the background before choosing the passer-by; a clean gap often matters more than another burst.
startingPoint: Test in the exact patch of light where the subject will be, then adjust ISO or its compensation.

title: Night street, handheld
conditions: After dark on a street with illuminated shop windows or pools of lamp light; pedestrians are moving.
intent: Keep people sharp and preserve the atmosphere of the street.

setup.focusTarget: Track the face as it reaches a lit area; use a small AF point on a contrast edge if eye detection fails.
setup.whiteBalance: 3800 K starting point; RAW if available
setup.stabilization: On for handheld; still hold steady.
setup.metering: Multi/evaluative as a reference; check important highlights in the test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Keep 1/250 s for walkers. Open to f/1.8 if available; let Auto ISO rise to 12800 before accepting motion blur. Seek brighter light if the ceiling is reached.

phone.mode: Photo mode for moving people
phone.aperture: Usually fixed by the selected lens; not user-adjustable.
phone.shutter: Automatic; 1/125–1/250 s if manual control exists
phone.focus: Tap the face when it enters a shop’s light.
phone.focal: Main 1× lens; avoid digital zoom.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto or around 3800 K in a manual app
phone.guidance: Stay close to a bright window and capture people as they pause; brace against a wall.
phone.limitation: Multi-second Night mode suits static streets but can erase or smear people; a phone may not freeze dark, fast-moving subjects.
why: A lit doorway supplies the face light that a phone cannot create by raising ISO alone.
A normal short capture handles people more predictably than a long Night sequence.
The main lens usually gives more useful low-light detail than a heavily cropped or dim telephoto view.
steps: Find a bright shop window or lamp illuminating faces from the side or front.
Use the main lens in Photo mode with flash off; leave unlit pavement dark.
Tap the face in the light and capture a short sequence at a pause in the stride.
Inspect the eye, moving feet and bright signs separately.
For a moving person, use a brighter position or a manual 1/250 s if available; accept more noise rather than assuming Night mode freezes movement.

essential: Phone with a clean main lens

problems.symptom: Face smears but signs are sharp
problems.cause: The person moved during the capture.
problems.fix: Wait for a pause or brighter light; use 1/250 s in a capable manual app.

problems.symptom: Every lamp has a doubled edge
problems.cause: The phone moved during exposure.
problems.fix: Brace elbows or lean safely against a wall; squeeze the release gently.

problems.cause: One or more colour channels clipped.
problems.fix: Lower exposure and inspect the lettering; choose a better-lit face if it becomes too dark.

problems.symptom: Person appears in pieces or disappears
problems.cause: Night processing merged different positions.
problems.fix: Use normal Photo mode for people; save Night mode for an empty static street.

phone.tip: A half-step into the window light often helps more than another zoom level.

why: The shutter protects people from blur; stabilization only helps camera movement.
f/2 admits enough light to keep the shutter usable, at the cost of a narrower focus margin.
Allowing dark pavement to stay dark stops the meter from over-brightening the whole scene.
steps: Find a well-lit patch with an uncluttered background.
Set RAW if supported and turn off flash.
Choose 1/250 s, f/2 and Auto ISO; set a realistic upper limit.
Focus on the person in the light and make several short bursts.
Inspect eyes, bright signs and the red/blue channels if your camera shows them.
If the face is underexposed at the ISO ceiling, wait for a brighter position or use f/1.8.

essential: Fast lens or main phone camera

problems.symptom: Face streaks while signs are sharp
problems.cause: Person moved during the exposure.
problems.fix: Use 1/500 s for brisk movement and accept higher ISO.

problems.cause: Hand movement, not focus.
problems.fix: Brace your stance and keep 1/250 s or faster.

problems.symptom: Face is soft but coat lettering is sharp
problems.cause: AF did not reach the eye.
problems.fix: Place a small AF point on the lit eye or nearest facial edge.

problems.cause: Bright channels clipped.
problems.fix: Lower exposure with Auto ISO compensation or manual ISO; do not judge only the average histogram.

alternatives.name: Static empty street
alternatives.effect: Clean architecture and intentional pedestrian ghosts.
alternatives.requirements: Tripod, static viewpoint and a timer.

alternatives.name: Quiet portrait in a doorway
alternatives.effect: A still person appears brighter with less ISO noise.
alternatives.requirements: Ask the subject to hold still in a lit doorway.

tip: Watch where a lamp catches the eyes; a half-step into that light can outperform a much more expensive lens.
startingPoint: Make a test as the person reaches the light; do not expose the whole frame to look like daylight.

title: Neon signs and coloured light
conditions: A bright neon or LED sign after dark; mostly static lettering against a much darker wall.
intent: Hold colour and letter shape without turning the tubes into white lines.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a distinct edge of the lettering; verify at magnification if reflections create a second edge.
setup.whiteBalance: 4000 K starting point; keep the chosen balance fixed
setup.stabilization: On for handheld; still hold steady.
setup.metering: Multi/evaluative as a reference; check important highlights in the test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Start here, then lower ISO toward 100 if the coloured letters clip. Keep 1/125 s unless the sign is flickering; test slower speeds or anti-flicker controls when bands appear.

phone.mode: Photo or manual/Pro mode
phone.iso: Auto; lower if manual controls exist
phone.aperture: Usually fixed by the selected lens; not user-adjustable.
phone.shutter: Auto; try 1/100 or 1/120 s for flicker only if adjustable
phone.focus: Tap the lettering and lower the exposure slider.
phone.focal: Main or true optical telephoto; no digital zoom.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance or select around 4000 K only if the app offers those controls.
phone.support: Handheld; support at slow shutter speeds
phone.guidance: Make one darker frame specifically for the lettering; inspect whether colours remain distinct.
phone.limitation: Some LED frequencies still produce bands; phones may provide no shutter fine-tuning or anti-flicker option.
why: A neon sign emits its own light, so exposing the surrounding darkness brightly can destroy the lettering.
A fixed or locked colour balance keeps related frames consistent when the app permits it.
Different LED refresh rates mean no single phone shutter speed cures every dark band.
steps: Clean the lens and choose a view where letters do not overlap distracting reflections.
Start in Photo mode, tap a lettering edge and reduce exposure until colours separate.
Make a test and enlarge the brightest coloured letters rather than judging only the dark wall.
If bands appear, try an available anti-flicker mode or a manual 1/100 or 1/120 s test; inspect the saved frame.
Support the phone for slower tests, and change position or capture mode if the sign still bands.

optional: Manual app with shutter and white-balance controls

problems.symptom: Letters are white instead of coloured
problems.cause: Exposure clipped the bright tubes.
problems.fix: Lower the exposure slider or manual ISO and retest the brightest letter.

problems.cause: LED timing interacts with the sensor readout.
problems.fix: Test supported anti-flicker or different shutter durations; there may be no clean setting on this phone.

problems.symptom: Large glow washes over the picture
problems.cause: Fingerprints, moisture or flare spread the light.
problems.fix: Clean and dry the lens, then change angle slightly.

problems.cause: Autofocus missed the letter boundary.
problems.fix: Tap an edge between a letter and its background; lock focus if offered.

phone.tip: Take one deliberately darker frame for the lettering before trying to brighten the wall.

why: The sign produces its own light, so night does not automatically mean very high ISO.
A moderate aperture keeps nearby lettering readable while still allowing a handheld shutter.
Fixed white balance keeps a series consistent; it cannot restore a clipped colour channel.
steps: Look for a sign with an interesting wall, reflection or surrounding negative space.
Clean the front element; bright tubes reveal fingerprints as flare.
Use single-point focus on a letter edge and take the starting frame.
Enlarge the letters and check each colour channel for clipping.
Lower ISO or stop down until coloured details return.
If horizontal bands appear, test mechanical shutter and suitable anti-flicker/variable shutter settings where available.

optional: Small support for longer shutter tests

problems.symptom: Red lettering becomes pale or white
problems.cause: The red channel is clipped.
problems.fix: Reduce ISO or shorten exposure until colour returns.

problems.symptom: Dark horizontal bars cross the sign
problems.cause: LED refresh and shutter timing interact.
problems.fix: Try mechanical shutter, anti-flicker or a tested slower exposure; no one speed fixes every LED.

problems.symptom: Letters have a glow across the frame
problems.cause: Fingerprints, condensation or strong flare.
problems.fix: Clean the lens and change angle slightly.

problems.symptom: Only the back wall is sharp
problems.cause: AF missed the low-detail bright tubes.
problems.fix: Focus on the border between a letter and the wall; magnify to confirm.

alternatives.name: Whole storefront
alternatives.effect: More surrounding detail and depth without losing the sign.
alternatives.requirements: Tripod or firm support; no moving subject.

alternatives.name: Reflected neon abstraction
alternatives.effect: A sharp reflection fragment against a softer foreground.
alternatives.requirements: Wet glass or puddle; focus on the reflected sign, not the surface.

tip: Turn the camera slightly until letters stop overlapping their reflections in the glass.
startingPoint: Test exposure on the brightest coloured lettering, then decide how much surrounding shadow to retain.

title: Traffic light trails
conditions: A fixed roadside viewpoint after blue hour, with moderate flowing traffic and dim ambient light.
intent: Draw continuous headlight and tail-light lines through a sharp city scene.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a distant lit road edge or building along the route, then switch to manual without moving the focus ring.
setup.whiteBalance: 3500–4500 K; choose one value for the series
setup.stabilization: Use tripod-compatible stabilization or switch it off as your lens manual directs.
setup.metering: Multi/evaluative as a reference; check important highlights in the test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Lengthen from 5 to 30 s for longer or denser trails. If buildings become too bright, lower ISO to base or stop down; an ND filter is optional only when ambient light is still too bright.

phone.mode: Manual long exposure or light-trail app, if supported
phone.aperture: Usually fixed by the selected lens; not user-adjustable.
phone.shutter: 5–15 s true exposure or app-composited equivalent
phone.focus: Lock focus on a distant building or road light.
phone.focal: Main 1× or ultrawide for a sweeping road.
phone.guidance: Use a dedicated long-exposure mode and trigger without moving the phone; inspect buildings for overexposure.
phone.limitation: A Night-mode stack may suppress moving cars instead of drawing trails. App composites do not behave exactly like one camera exposure.
why: A rigid phone position keeps buildings sharp while vehicle lights move.
A genuine slow exposure and a frame-blended trail mode can produce different trail continuity.
Ordinary Night mode may remove passing vehicles, so its long countdown does not guarantee light trails.
steps: Choose a permitted pavement viewpoint where a curve or junction gives the lights a clear path.
Clamp the phone securely and select a documented light-trail mode or manual long exposure.
Lock focus on a distant building; lock exposure and white balance when the mode allows.
Start a 5–15 s capture or the app’s trail interval as traffic approaches, without touching the support.
Inspect building detail, trail gaps and headlight clipping; adjust the mode’s duration or brightness controls and make another pass.

essential: Phone with a supported light-trail or long-exposure app

problems.symptom: Cars disappear instead of leaving lines
problems.cause: The selected Night stack suppressed moving objects.
problems.fix: Use a documented trail mode or true slow exposure; a normal Night capture may not produce this effect.

problems.cause: The support moved during the sequence.
problems.fix: Use solid ground and a timer; avoid flexible railings and touching the clamp.

problems.symptom: Headlights become a broad white band
problems.cause: Too many bright passes accumulated or exposure is excessive.
problems.fix: Shorten the trail interval, reduce exposure where supported or wait for lighter traffic.

problems.cause: The app captured separated frames or vehicles stopped.
problems.fix: Use a continuous trail mode if available and choose flowing traffic; some apps cannot remove capture gaps.

phone.tip: Test the capture mode on one passing car before committing to a long traffic sequence.

why: Fifteen seconds gives passing vehicles time to cross a useful length of the frame.
f/8 keeps roadside architecture and distant lights sufficiently defined without defaulting to f/22.
A low fixed ISO keeps the bright trails from clipping and makes repeated frames comparable.
steps: Choose a legal pavement or enclosed viewpoint with a strong curve or converging road lines.
Place the tripod where it cannot obstruct anyone and frame clear of streetlight glare.
Focus on a distant lit edge and lock manual focus.
Set a timer or remote, then start a 15 s exposure as traffic approaches.
Inspect trail continuity, building highlights and vibration in the architecture.
Adjust the exposure duration for traffic density, compensating with aperture or ISO only within useful limits.

problems.symptom: Buildings are sharp but trails are too short
problems.cause: Exposure ended before vehicles crossed the frame.
problems.fix: Try 20–30 s or wait for slower traffic.

problems.symptom: Every building has tiny repeated edges
problems.cause: Tripod vibration, wind or footsteps on the platform.
problems.fix: Move to solid ground, shorten the centre column and use a timer.

problems.symptom: White traffic bands cover the road
problems.cause: Too many bright headlights accumulated.
problems.fix: Shorten to 5–8 s or choose a quieter gap; stop down one stop if necessary.

problems.symptom: The road is empty in the image
problems.cause: Cars passed outside the exposure or stacking removed them.
problems.fix: Time a true long exposure with visible traffic; check the phone mode’s treatment of movement.

alternatives.name: Sparse individual trails
alternatives.effect: Separate ribbons with visible road between them.
alternatives.requirements: A few vehicles at a time.

alternatives.name: Dense ribbons
alternatives.effect: More continuous traffic and stronger light-star points.
alternatives.requirements: Darker ambient light and a rigid tripod; avoid a very bright headlight stream.

tip: A road bending toward the camera gives more depth than a straight line across the frame.
startingPoint: Start with one test pass; traffic volume can change brightness more than the sky does.
safety: Work from a legal safe pavement or enclosed viewpoint; never stand in a carriageway or set equipment where it obstructs traffic.

title: Blue-hour skyline
conditions: Buildings have switched on their lights while the twilight sky is still visibly blue; the skyline is static.
intent: Balance warm city lights with a coloured sky and clean architectural detail.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a high-contrast lit edge within the main skyline; enlarge a frame to confirm the distant detail.
setup.whiteBalance: 4000–4500 K for a blue sky and warm lights
setup.stabilization: Use tripod-compatible stabilization or switch it off as your lens manual directs.
setup.metering: Multi/evaluative as a reference; check important highlights in the test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Adjust shutter from 1 to 15 s as twilight fades; leave ISO low and aperture near f/8. Take another test every few minutes because the sky is changing.

phone.mode: Night mode for the static skyline
phone.aperture: Usually fixed by the selected lens; not user-adjustable.
phone.shutter: Automatic multi-frame capture; hold for the displayed duration
phone.focus: Tap a distant building and keep the phone still.
phone.focal: Main 1×; optical telephoto only with enough light.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto or fixed around 4200 K if controllable
phone.guidance: Lower the exposure slider slightly if building lights lose detail and let the capture finish.
phone.limitation: The displayed Night-mode duration is a capture sequence, not necessarily one exposure; it may alter clouds and water.
why: Twilight lets the phone record sky colour and building lights within a more manageable brightness range.
A supported Night capture suits a static skyline, although clouds and water can change during processing.
Keeping the phone level avoids spending much of the image on later perspective correction.
steps: Arrive while the sky is still visibly blue and choose an unobstructed skyline.
Use the main lens, level the phone and tap a distant building.
Brace or mount the phone and compare ordinary Photo mode with a supported Night capture.
Inspect windows, sky colour and the corners of the skyline at full size.
Lower exposure if windows bleach; repeat every few minutes as the sky changes rather than keeping one setting all evening.

essential: Stable support or a steady safe stance

problems.symptom: Sky is black and windows dominate
problems.cause: The useful twilight balance has passed.
problems.fix: Try earlier on the next visit; simply brightening now will also brighten the windows.

problems.cause: Exposure prioritised shadows over bright lights.
problems.fix: Lower the exposure slider and compare a normal Photo frame.

problems.cause: Multi-frame processing handled movement unevenly.
problems.fix: Try ordinary Photo mode or a documented long-exposure app; inspect the saved water detail.

problems.cause: The phone was tilted upward.
problems.fix: Keep the sensor plane vertical, step back where safe and leave space for modest correction.

phone.tip: Keep a few frames from different moments; the best sky-to-window balance changes quickly.

why: Twilight reduces the difference between the sky and artificial lights, avoiding a black empty sky.
f/8 is a practical detail setting when the subject is distant and movement is unimportant.
Shutter time can change freely on a solid support, so ISO need not rise with the fading light.
steps: Arrive before the lights and choose a clean horizon with no foreground poles crossing key buildings.
Level the camera; decide whether reflections strengthen the arrangement.
Focus on the skyline, then lock focus for repeated frames.
Take a 4 s test at f/8 and ISO 100.
Check the brightest windows and whether the sky still has colour.
Shorten the exposure if lights clip; lengthen as the sky darkens and capture several balances.

problems.symptom: Sky is black while windows are bright
problems.cause: The useful twilight balance has passed.
problems.fix: Return earlier on another evening; a brighter exposure alone will clip lights.

problems.cause: Camera was tilted upward.
problems.fix: Level the camera or step farther back and leave cropping room.

problems.symptom: Skyline is soft in every frame
problems.cause: Focus landed nearby or tripod moved.
problems.fix: Magnify a distant edge, refocus, then check for vibration separately.

problems.symptom: City is orange but the sky is grey
problems.cause: White balance is too warm or automatic balance shifted.
problems.fix: Try a fixed value near 4200 K and compare a RAW adjustment.

alternatives.name: Earlier twilight
alternatives.effect: Brighter blue sky with subtler window lights.
alternatives.requirements: Shoot while there is more ambient light.

alternatives.name: Water smoothed under skyline
alternatives.effect: Soft reflections contrast with sharp buildings.
alternatives.requirements: Calm viewpoint after more light has faded; shorten if highlights clip.

tip: Make several frames a few minutes apart; the strongest colour balance may last less time than setting up the tripod.
startingPoint: The 4 s exposure is an initial test; twilight brightness depends on cloud, season, latitude and direction.

title: Tall buildings and straight verticals
conditions: A sunlit or bright-overcast building viewed from street level; the structure is static and vertical lines matter.
intent: Keep the facade sharp and make a deliberate choice about converging verticals.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a window frame around the central facade; check both nearby and distant edges if the building recedes.
setup.whiteBalance: Daylight or Auto WB
setup.stabilization: On for handheld; still hold steady.
setup.metering: Multi/evaluative as a reference; check important highlights in the test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Use f/8 for detail. In overcast light raise ISO to 200–400 before handholding slower than your tested limit. Keep the camera level for parallel verticals; exposure cannot correct perspective.

phone.mode: Photo mode with grid/level
phone.aperture: Usually fixed by the selected lens; not user-adjustable.
phone.shutter: Automatic; brace in shade
phone.focus: Tap the central facade.
phone.focal: Main 1× if you can step back; ultrawide for restricted space.
phone.guidance: Keep the phone vertical and level rather than tipping it upward; leave extra room for perspective correction.
phone.limitation: Ultrawide edges stretch nearby features. Software correction crops the frame and cannot reveal a missing roof.
why: Tilting the phone upward makes verticals converge even when the lens itself is well corrected.
The main lens from farther away usually gives more restrained edge proportions than a close ultrawide view.
Straightening later crops the frame, so missing roof space cannot be repaired by a setting.
steps: Find a permitted viewpoint with enough distance and clear roof space.
Enable the grid or level and start with the main lens.
Keep the phone’s sensor plane vertical, tap facade detail and make a test.
Check both side edges, roof clearance and bright stone or glass.
If the whole building cannot fit, choose intentional upward convergence or a wider view with correction space; do not assume exposure changes will straighten it.

essential: Phone with a grid or level display

problems.cause: The phone tilted upward.
problems.fix: Level it and move back where safe, or label the converging view as an intentional composition.

problems.cause: A very close wide viewpoint exaggerates proportions.
problems.fix: Step back and use the main lens; keep important details away from extreme corners.

problems.cause: The original frame left no correction margin.
problems.fix: Reshoot wider with more space above and beside the facade.

problems.cause: Highlights clipped.
problems.fix: Reduce exposure and inspect the actual wall or glass, not just the overall screen brightness.

phone.tip: Watch a vertical near each edge; they reveal small camera tilts better than a busy centre.

why: Camera tilt, rather than focal length alone, makes verticals converge.
f/8 provides useful facade depth and edge performance without an unnecessarily tiny aperture.
A slightly wider frame leaves room for straightening, but moving back produces a less exaggerated near/far relationship.
steps: Choose a viewpoint where street furniture does not merge with the facade.
Stand back or gain elevation where access permits.
Level the camera and use a grid to align prominent verticals.
Focus on a facade detail and make the starting exposure.
Inspect corners, roof clearance and bright stonework.
If the roof will not fit, choose intentional convergence or a shift lens; leave correction space rather than cutting it off.

essential: Camera or phone with grid display
optional: Polarizer only after checking uneven sky and reflections

problems.cause: Camera pointed upward.
problems.fix: Level it and move back, use a shift lens, or correct moderately from a wider frame.

problems.cause: Very close viewpoint with a wide field of view.
problems.fix: Move farther away and use a longer focal length.

problems.symptom: Window detail is soft only at one depth
problems.cause: Insufficient depth of field or wrong focus plane.
problems.fix: Focus between important planes and try f/11; inspect again.

problems.cause: Sunlit material overexposed.
problems.fix: Lower ISO or shorten shutter; inspect highlight warnings on the material.

alternatives.name: Deliberate upward drama
alternatives.effect: Strong converging lines lead toward the roof.
alternatives.requirements: Centre the camera carefully and make the tilt visibly intentional.

alternatives.name: Facade detail study
alternatives.effect: Patterns and surface texture fill the frame.
alternatives.requirements: A 70–135 mm-equivalent lens and a more distant viewpoint.

tip: Watch the nearest vertical at the edge of the frame; it reveals small tilts more clearly than a busy centre.
startingPoint: Check both exposure and geometry in the first frame; they require different corrections.

title: Cathedral and church interiors
conditions: A dim, largely static interior with bright windows; photography and support use are permitted.
intent: Show the depth and rhythm of the architecture while retaining important illuminated detail.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a contrast edge partway into the nave; enlarge a foreground column and distant altar to check depth.
setup.whiteBalance: Auto WB in RAW; mixed light rarely has one perfect value
setup.stabilization: Use tripod-compatible stabilization or switch it off as your lens manual directs.
setup.metering: Multi/evaluative as a reference; check important highlights in the test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Keep f/8 where depth matters and lengthen shutter on support. If windows clip, capture a darker frame by shortening shutter; do not raise ISO just to brighten the nave.

phone.mode: Night mode for a static interior
phone.aperture: Usually fixed by the selected lens; not user-adjustable.
phone.shutter: Automatic multi-frame sequence
phone.focus: Tap a mid-distance column or arch.
phone.focal: Main 1×; ultrawide if necessary.
phone.guidance: Keep verticals straight and hold still through the whole capture; make a darker frame for stained glass.
phone.limitation: Tripods or flash may be prohibited, and a bright window can exceed the phone’s recoverable range even with HDR.
why: A supported Night capture can reveal a static interior without using prohibited flash.
Bright stained glass may exceed the room exposure even when automatic HDR is active.
A level main-lens view keeps the architecture believable; an ultrawide view needs careful edge checks.
steps: Check photography and support rules before choosing a position; keep flash off.

title: Candlelit face
conditions: A person sitting quietly near several candles in an otherwise dim room.
intent: Preserve warm facial light and atmosphere without making the person a silhouette.

setup.focus: AF-S or eye AF · lit eye
setup.focusTarget: Focus on the nearer lit eye; if the camera hunts, use a small point on the eyelid and verify at magnification.
setup.whiteBalance: 2800–3200 K; keep some warmth
setup.stabilization: On for handheld; still hold steady.
setup.metering: Multi/evaluative as a reference; check important highlights in the test frame.
setup.exposureNote: At 1/100 s ask the person to stay still. Raise ISO toward 6400 before using a much slower exposure; open only if your lens and focus accuracy permit. The tiny flame cores may clip while the face remains correctly exposed.

phone.mode: Photo mode near the candles; short Night capture only for a very still person
phone.aperture: Usually fixed by the selected lens; not user-adjustable.
phone.shutter: Automatic; hold both camera and subject still
phone.focus: Tap the lit eye or face.
phone.focal: Main 1× lens; avoid a dim telephoto.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; reduce excessive orange only if controllable
phone.guidance: Move the face closer to the light without putting hair or clothing near flame; tap the face and reduce exposure if skin highlights bleach.
phone.limitation: Long Night sequences can smear blinking eyes and moving flames; a fixed phone aperture cannot be opened further.
why: Moving the face safely into useful candlelight improves exposure more than making the dark room look bright.
The face and flame need different treatment; a tiny clipped flame core may be acceptable when skin remains detailed.
A long Night sequence can blur blinking eyes and merge changing flames even when the phone is supported.
steps: Secure candles away from hair, fabric and the table edge before arranging the portrait.
Use the main lens and place the face where it receives light without approaching the flame dangerously.
Tap the lit eye or face and start with ordinary Photo mode.
Ask for a brief pause and make several frames; try a short supported Night capture only for a genuinely still subject.
Inspect the eye and bright skin; add safely placed light or change face position if the image is too dark.
Keep some warmth and surrounding darkness rather than lifting every shadow.

essential: Stable candle holders and a safe supervised arrangement
optional: White reflector kept safely clear of flames

problems.cause: Exposure was dominated by the flame.
problems.fix: Tap the face and increase exposure cautiously, or bring more safe light to the face.

problems.symptom: Eye blurs but candle holder is sharp
problems.cause: The person moved during capture.
problems.fix: Use a shorter normal capture in brighter face light and ask for a brief pause.

problems.cause: Night processing combined different flame positions.
problems.fix: Compare ordinary Photo mode and keep the frame with cleaner flame and eye detail.

problems.symptom: Skin is uniformly orange and muddy
problems.cause: Weak exposure or colour processing obscured variation.
problems.fix: Improve actual face light first; adjust WB in a capable app or edit while keeping natural warmth.

phone.tip: Turn the face slightly toward the brightest safe candle position until a catchlight appears.

why: A wide aperture and moderately fast shutter help a living person stay sharp in weak light.
Candle placement changes facial light much more than a small white-balance adjustment.
A little clipping in a tiny flame core may be acceptable; do not sacrifice the face merely to make every flame pixel dark.
steps: Place candles securely away from hair, fabric and the edge of a table.
Arrange the face close enough to receive light with one side slightly brighter.
Brace the camera and focus on the nearer lit eye.
Ask for a brief pause and take a 1/100 s test.
Enlarge the eye and inspect bright skin, not only the flame.
Add another safely placed candle or raise ISO if the face is too dark; avoid relying on a long shutter.

essential: Fast lens or main phone camera
optional: Reflector/white card kept clear of flame

problems.cause: Exposure was set only for the flame.
problems.fix: Increase exposure for the face and accept a small clipped core, or bring more light to the face.

problems.symptom: Eyes blur but candle holder is sharp

problems.fix: Use 1/125–1/200 s and raise ISO.

problems.cause: Very shallow focus depth or wrong AF target.
problems.fix: Refocus on the eye and use f/2.2 if enough light exists.

problems.symptom: Skin is strongly orange with little variation
problems.cause: White balance too warm or face severely underexposed.
problems.fix: Try 2800–3200 K in RAW and improve actual light on the face.

alternatives.name: More facial depth

alternatives.name: Flame detail only

title: People beside a campfire
conditions: People gathered near a controlled campfire after dark, with irregular flickering light and small gestures.
intent: Record warm faces, some flame structure and the feeling of the gathering.

setup.focusTarget: Track the face nearest the useful firelight; avoid letting the flame become the AF target.
setup.whiteBalance: 3000–3500 K; RAW if available
setup.stabilization: On for handheld; still hold steady.
setup.metering: Multi/evaluative as a reference; check important highlights in the test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Use 1/250 s for gestures and changing flame structure. Raise ISO if the face is too dark; if the fire overwhelms the scene, reframe or wait for lower flames rather than underexposing every face.

phone.mode: Photo mode; use short bursts at brighter flickers
phone.aperture: Usually fixed by the selected lens; not user-adjustable.
phone.shutter: Automatic; no long Night capture for moving faces
phone.focus: Tap a face when it catches the firelight.
phone.focal: Main 1× lens
phone.support: Handheld or braced well away from the fire
phone.guidance: Photograph the brighter flicker and a pause in conversation together; include enough darkness to retain the night mood.
phone.limitation: The phone may blend changing flames or smear faces. Small bright flame cores can exceed the available dynamic range.
why: Firelight changes between frames, so a brighter flicker and a still expression need to coincide.
The main phone lens is a practical low-light choice for people and their surroundings.
Exposing every flame perfectly can leave all faces black; decide which part tells the story.
steps: Choose a safe position clear of sparks, smoke and movement around the fire.
Use the main lens in Photo mode with flash off unless a permitted fill-light result is specifically wanted.
Tap a face when a brighter flicker reaches it; keep large flames from blocking the face.
Capture short sequences during a pause in conversation.
Inspect face sharpness and bright skin, then decide how much flame clipping is acceptable.
Move to a safer clearer angle or wait for lower flames instead of asking people to approach the fire.

problems.cause: Automatic exposure prioritised the flames.
problems.fix: Tap a lit face and adjust exposure or reframe toward better-lit people.

problems.cause: The firelight changed.
problems.fix: Capture several short sequences around brighter flickers and select a balanced frame.

problems.cause: Movement and multi-frame processing interacted.
problems.fix: Use normal Photo mode and a pause; long Night capture is poorly suited to this moment.

problems.symptom: A pale veil covers the image
problems.cause: Smoke or flare crossed the view.
problems.fix: Change to a safe clearer angle and clean the lens; keep well away from sparks.

phone.tip: Watch the people and the flame together; the best exposure moment may arrive between the biggest flames.

why: The flickering fire makes exposure vary from frame to frame, so timing is part of the setup.
1/250 s is faster than a static candle portrait because gestures and flames are more active.
A wider view keeps the group and fire related without making one face the whole story.
steps: Choose a safe position clear of smoke, sparks and people moving around the fire.
Frame faces on the far side or side of the fire without the largest flames blocking them.
Track a lit face and set the starting exposure.
Shoot short bursts as a brighter flicker illuminates the group.
Inspect face sharpness and whether large flame areas have lost all detail.
Reframe, wait for a lower flame or change exposure according to whether faces or flame are the main subject.

problems.symptom: Faces are black around a detailed fire
problems.cause: Exposure favoured the flames.
problems.fix: Increase exposure for faces, move the composition toward better-lit people or use a little permitted fill light.

problems.cause: Firelight changed between frames.
problems.fix: Shoot short bursts around brighter flickers and choose a balanced frame.

problems.cause: Smoke crossed the lens or flare spread from the fire.
problems.fix: Move to a safe clearer angle and use a hood; do not move closer to the fire.

problems.symptom: People have blurred hands but sharp chairs
problems.cause: Subject movement.
problems.fix: Keep 1/250 s or use 1/500 s and more ISO.

alternatives.name: Fire and spark patterns
alternatives.effect: Flame tongues and sparks become more defined; people darken.
alternatives.requirements: Frame the fire as the subject from a safe distance.

alternatives.name: Still group by a low fire
alternatives.effect: Faces receive more exposure with less frozen flame detail.
alternatives.requirements: Ask people for a brief pause and keep precise face focus.

tip: Wait for someone to lean into the light naturally; do not ask them to move dangerously close to improve exposure.
startingPoint: Take several tests across different flickers; one frame cannot describe the whole firelight cycle.
safety: Respect local fire restrictions; keep equipment, people and flammable clothing clear of flames and sparks, and do not obstruct safe movement.

title: Speaker under a spotlight
conditions: A speaker under a bright stage spotlight with a dark background and occasional hand gestures.
intent: Render the face and gesture clearly while letting unlit areas remain dark.

setup.focusTarget: Track the speaker’s nearer eye; if the lectern blocks the face, use a small point on the visible facial edge.
setup.whiteBalance: 3200–4500 K according to the key light; RAW
setup.stabilization: On for handheld; still hold steady.
setup.metering: Multi/evaluative as a reference; check important highlights in the test frame.
setup.exposureNote: The face, not the dark background, sets exposure. Reduce ISO if skin clips; use 1/500 s for emphatic hand gestures. Keep f/4 where possible for a useful face-to-hand depth margin.

phone.mode: Photo mode; flash off
phone.aperture: Usually fixed by the selected lens; not user-adjustable.
phone.shutter: Automatic; capture a pause in gesture
phone.focus: Tap the lit face and lower exposure if skin goes white.
phone.focal: True optical telephoto if light permits; otherwise a wider contextual view.
phone.guidance: Hold exposure on the speaker instead of the projected slide; wait for an expressive face and unobstructed hands.
phone.limitation: A distant small face may exceed phone reach; screen projections and spotlights may also exceed one frame’s brightness range.
why: A dark stage should remain dark when the face is lit; exposing for the whole room can bleach the speaker.
A pause in speech or gesture helps a phone hold a distant face.
Optical reach and actual face detail matter more than a large digital zoom number.
steps: Choose an approved view where the microphone does not cover the mouth.
Use Photo mode with flash off; try a real telephoto only if it keeps useful detail.
Tap the lit face and lower exposure until forehead and cheek texture remain.
Capture a short sequence at a clear expression or a held gesture.
Enlarge the face, inspect hand movement and look for LED bands.
For audience or slides, make a separate composition exposed for that subject rather than brightening the speaker’s frame indiscriminately.

problems.symptom: Face turns white while the stage looks bright
problems.cause: The exposure lifted the dark surroundings too far.

problems.symptom: Hands streak while the face is defined
problems.cause: Gesture speed exceeded the capture.
problems.fix: Wait for the held part of a gesture or use a supported faster shutter in sufficient light.

problems.symptom: Slide and face cannot both be readable
problems.cause: Their brightness or focus needs differ.
problems.fix: Take separate slide and speaker frames; one global exposure may not preserve both.

phone.tip: A hand held clear of the mouth often communicates the speech better than a rapid blurred gesture.

why: A dark backdrop can fool automatic metering into making the face too bright.
f/4 provides a little more depth for a turning head and nearby hands than a wide-open portrait.
1/250 s handles speech movements while keeping ISO lower than a faster action setup.
steps: Find an approved angle with the microphone clear of the mouth.
Watch where the speaker pauses and which side receives the key light.
Focus on the eye and take a test under the actual spotlight.
Check forehead and cheek highlights, then lower ISO if they clip.
Wait for a clear gesture and expression, using short bursts.
If slides matter, make a separate frame exposed for them rather than forcing both into one poor exposure.

problems.symptom: Face is white, background looks normal
problems.cause: Exposure was lifted for the dark backdrop.
problems.fix: Lower ISO or shorten shutter and let the backdrop stay dark.

problems.symptom: Hands blur but eyes are sharp
problems.cause: Gestures are faster than head movement.
problems.fix: Try 1/500 s and raise ISO.

problems.cause: Projection and face require different exposures or focus.
problems.fix: Take a separate slide frame or change viewpoint to reduce the contrast.

alternatives.name: Tight expressive gesture
alternatives.effect: A faster moment is isolated from the background.
alternatives.requirements: Bright key light and precise continuous focus.

Turn the person toward the bright sky until both eyes receive light.
Use the main lens or a genuine portrait telephoto in enough light, stepping back to a comfortable distance.

Inspect both eyes, hair and glasses; reduce simulated blur or use the normal frame if edges fail.

why: Open sky acts as a broad light source, giving softer transitions than direct sun.

Turn the person toward open sky until both eyes have a catchlight.
Place the background well behind them and check for bright distractions.
Focus on the nearer eye and make a short first sequence.

essential: Open shade with sky in front

why: HDR can change shadow brightness but cannot remove squinting or move an awkward nose shadow.

A fixed phone aperture makes position and exposure adjustment more useful than a camera-style f-stop prescription.

Move the face or camera until hard brow and nose shadows have a deliberate shape.
Use Photo mode, tap the face and reduce exposure if the lit cheek loses texture.

essential: Comfortable safe position for the subject

problems.cause: Skin highlights clipped.

problems.cause: HDR or portrait processing struggled with extreme contrast.

why: A short shutter handles bright light without forcing a tiny aperture.

Check the nose and brow shadows on the face.
Set base ISO and take the fast-shutter starting frame.

Look for open sky or a neutral wall lighting the face.
Focus on the near eye and take a starting frame.
Inspect skin detail, eye contrast and unwanted flare shapes.
Adjust ISO for the face; use a reflector or change angle if the brightness range remains too great.

problems.cause: Exposure followed the bright background.

Use the main lens in Photo mode and get to a useful eye-level viewpoint.

problems.cause: Water absorbed warm wavelengths over depth and distance.
problems.fix: Shoot shallower and nearer; use available underwater WB within its limits, without promising missing colours will return.

problems.symptom: Image stays hazy despite apparent focus
problems.cause: Too much suspended material or water lies between lens and subject.
problems.fix: Choose clearer water and a nearer composition without disturbing marine life.

problems.cause: Drift or subject motion exceeded the capture speed.
problems.fix: Stabilise buoyancy and seek brighter shallow light; a supported manual app may use 1/250–1/500 s.

problems.symptom: Housing fogs, leaks or controls fail
problems.cause: Preparation, sealing or operating conditions are unsuitable.
problems.fix: Stop photography and exit safely; follow the housing manufacturer’s instructions before using it again.

phone.tip: Practise every needed control with the housing dry; a touch gesture that works ashore may not work underwater.

why: Water between lens and subject reduces contrast and colour, so a nearby composition is more effective than distant zooming.
A wide view helps include the environment while keeping the camera reasonably close.
1/250 s limits swimmer drift and modest animal movement.
Custom white balance can improve available colour, but added light or a shallower scene is needed when red light is strongly lost.
steps: Inspect, assemble and test the rated housing exactly as its manufacturer directs.
Confirm safe entry, conditions, depth limits and your own swimming/diving competence.
Choose a nearby subject without approaching or disturbing it aggressively.
Keep buoyancy controlled, focus through the port and take the starting exposure.
Inspect highlights, contrast and sharpness when safe to do so.
Move to clearer/shallower water or reduce the water path if colours are weak; change ISO or aperture for exposure without neglecting safety.

optional: Underwater strobe and training for its use

problems.symptom: Scene is blue-green with weak reds

problems.symptom: Image is hazy despite correct focus

title: Ferry wake and moving-deck seascape
conditions: A moving passenger boat in bright daylight, with vibration, spray and a foaming wake behind it.
intent: Freeze wake texture and keep a level horizon despite the moving platform.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a defined part of the wake beyond the immediate spray; for a distant shoreline frame, focus on a shoreline feature instead.
setup.whiteBalance: Daylight
setup.stabilization: On for handheld; still hold steady.
setup.metering: Multi/evaluative as a reference; check important highlights in the test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Use 1/1000 s to resist deck vibration and hold foam detail. Lower ISO in stronger sun; raise it under cloud. A tripod on the boat does not remove the boat’s movement.

phone.mode: Photo mode with short bursts
phone.aperture: Usually fixed by the selected lens; not user-adjustable.
phone.shutter: Automatic; choose bright light and avoid long exposures
phone.focus: Tap the wake beyond nearby spray or the distant shoreline.
phone.focal: Main or ultrawide for wake-leading lines.
phone.guidance: Brace your body safely without pressing the phone against a vibrating rail; keep the horizon level and shoot between splashes.
phone.limitation: Stabilization cannot fully remove boat movement in a long exposure; water droplets on the lens can ruin every frame.
why: The boat is moving beneath the camera, so a tripod cannot provide a stationary long-exposure viewpoint.
Bright daylight helps a phone freeze foam and platform vibration.
The wake supplies strong leading lines while a level horizon keeps the view coherent.
steps: Choose a permitted passenger position with secure footing and attach a suitable strap or grip.
Clean spray from the lens and use Photo mode with the main or appropriate ultrawide lens.
Frame the wake without leaning beyond railings and tap defined foam beyond the immediate spray.
Take short bursts between splashes while keeping the horizon level.
Inspect foam texture, horizon and droplet blur.
For persistent smear, seek brighter light or use a supported manual 1/1000 s; protect footing and equipment before making adjustments.

essential: Phone with a secure grip or strap

problems.cause: Boat movement exceeded the capture speed.
problems.fix: Use a short normal capture in good light; do not switch to a long Night mode or rely on a deck-mounted tripod.

problems.symptom: Wake is a blank white shape
problems.cause: Foam highlights clipped.
problems.fix: Lower exposure and inspect foam detail while keeping a usable sea tone.

problems.cause: Boat roll changed the framing.
problems.fix: Use the grid or level and leave small straightening margins.

problems.cause: Spray landed on the lens.
problems.fix: Clean and shield the lens safely, then take another test.

phone.tip: Wait for the boat to straighten for a symmetrical wake, or use a turn’s curve deliberately.

why: A fast shutter controls both foam movement and movement of the camera platform.
f/8 gives useful depth from the wake into the distant scene.
The wake naturally forms converging lines, so a level horizon and balanced frame strengthen the result.
steps: Choose a permitted deck position with secure footing and keep clear of working crew.
Attach a strap and clean any spray from the lens.
Frame the wake as a leading line without leaning beyond a railing.
Focus beyond the near spray and make a short test burst.
Inspect foam detail, horizon level and droplet blur.
Use a faster shutter for remaining smear and reframe for changing boat direction.

essential: Camera or phone with secure strap

problems.symptom: Entire frame vibrates despite a tripod
problems.cause: The platform itself is moving.
problems.fix: Handhold safely with a fast shutter; do not rely on a tripod to stabilise the boat.

problems.symptom: Wake is a white blank shape
problems.cause: Foam highlights clipped.
problems.fix: Shorten exposure or lower ISO while retaining enough shadow detail.

problems.cause: Boat roll or unlevel framing.
problems.fix: Use the level/grid and leave small crop margins.

problems.symptom: Soft circles appear over the sea
problems.cause: Spray droplets on the front element.
problems.fix: Clean and shield the lens; take another test before continuing.

alternatives.name: Frozen spray detail
alternatives.effect: Individual splashes become more distinct.
alternatives.requirements: Bright light and a safe dry viewpoint; avoid moving closer to spray.

alternatives.name: Distant coastline from deck
alternatives.effect: A tighter shore view with less foreground wake.
alternatives.requirements: Use a 70–135 mm-equivalent view and retest sharpness at the longer focal length.

tip: Wait for the boat to straighten after a turn if you want a symmetrical wake; use the curve deliberately if it adds direction.
startingPoint: Take a test after changing deck position because vibration, spray and light can all change.
safety: Stay within passenger areas, keep secure footing and equipment, obey crew instructions and never lean beyond safety railings.

title: City overlook through glass
conditions: A city view through observation-deck glass in bright overcast light, with interior reflections and possible tinting.
intent: Record a clear distant city view while controlling reflections from the room behind you.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a distant building edge through the glass; check that the AF point did not settle on smudges or reflected lights.
setup.whiteBalance: Auto WB in RAW; tinted glass may require correction
setup.stabilization: On for handheld; still hold steady.
setup.metering: Multi/evaluative as a reference; check important highlights in the test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Use 1/250 s handheld. Raise ISO through dark tint or open to f/4; if the scene is static and support is allowed, a slower exposure is possible. Keep the lens close to the pane without stressing it.

phone.mode: Photo mode; flash off
phone.aperture: Usually fixed by the selected lens; not user-adjustable.
phone.shutter: Automatic; Night mode only for a stable after-dark view
phone.focus: Tap a distant building and lock focus if reflections interfere.
phone.focal: Main or true optical telephoto; choose a tighter clear section.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto WB; tinted glass can retain a colour cast
phone.guidance: Move close to a clean pane, shade the lens from room lights and avoid reflecting your screen or clothing.
phone.limitation: A polarizer may help at some angles but can reveal stress patterns in laminated glass; phone accessories are not a guaranteed cure.
why: Blocking reflected interior light is more effective than trying to remove it with exposure changes.
A main or genuine optical telephoto view can isolate a clear section of pane without heavy digital zoom.
Tint and multiple glass layers may limit colour and detail even when the phone is correctly focused.
steps: Choose a clean permitted pane and an angle with fewer reflected interior lamps.
Switch flash off, dim the screen and move close without stressing or touching the glass unnecessarily.
Shade the lens from room light with dark clothing or a hand kept outside the image.
Tap a distant building and make an ordinary Photo test.
Enlarge city detail, ghost reflections and colour casts.
Change position for reflections; after dark use a supported Night capture only when the scene and viewpoint are sufficiently still.

optional: Soft hood compatible with the phone

problems.cause: Interior lamps reflect in the pane.
problems.fix: Shade the lens and move to a darker section or a different angle.

problems.cause: Autofocus selected the glass.
problems.fix: Tap a distant building edge and lock focus if available.

problems.cause: An accessory polarizer interacts with laminated or stressed glass.
problems.fix: Remove it or test another angle while inspecting the whole frame.

problems.symptom: The city has a blue-green cast
problems.cause: Window tint changed the transmitted light.
problems.fix: Use available WB/tint correction or RAW editing, accepting that some colour may remain limited.

phone.tip: Dim the screen before blaming the glass; the reflection can be your own display.

why: The distant skyline needs little focus depth, so a moderate aperture is enough while helping hide nearby marks.
Reflections are a light-path problem; exposure changes do not remove a reflected lamp from the composition.
A tighter view can exclude window frames and tell a clearer city story than trying to fit the entire panorama.
steps: Find a clean pane and an angle with fewer interior lights reflected in it.
Turn flash off and dim the screen if it reflects in the glass.
Shade the lens with a hood or dark clothing without obstructing others.
Focus on a distant building and take a test.
Inspect the skyline detail, ghost reflections and colour cast.
Move position to remove reflections; adjust ISO or aperture for tint-related light loss.

optional: Lens cloth for your own lens only

problems.symptom: Ceiling lights float over the skyline
problems.cause: Interior reflections.
problems.fix: Shade the lens and move to a darker nearby pane or a different angle.

problems.cause: Focus landed on the glass.
problems.fix: Use a small AF point on distant detail or manual magnified focus.

problems.cause: Polarization interacting with laminated/stressed glass.
problems.fix: Remove or rotate the polarizer and check the whole frame.

problems.symptom: View is blue-green despite correct exposure
problems.cause: Tinted glass alters colour.
problems.fix: Use RAW and a careful WB/tint correction; some colour information may remain limited.

alternatives.name: After-dark glass view
alternatives.effect: Lit buildings remain readable with more noise.
alternatives.requirements: Strong bracing or permitted support; carefully block interior reflections.

alternatives.name: Compressed city detail
alternatives.effect: A tighter cluster of streets or buildings fills the frame.
alternatives.requirements: Use 85–135 mm-equivalent framing and a clear pane.

tip: Turn the screen brightness down before blaming the glass; sometimes the reflection is your own display.
startingPoint: Check the first frame for reflections at full size, then solve their source or viewpoint before changing exposure.
